title: Predictive GPU Scale & Eviction Playbook
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Summary

This playbook defines Redwood's recommended approach for predictive scaling and graceful eviction of GPU-backed inference workloads. It describes the architecture, metrics and dashboards, alerting thresholds, operational runbook for incidents, and a short retrospective checklist for continuous improvement. This doc is intended for platform engineers, SREs, and owners of the gpu-orchestrator, scheduler-api, and capacity services.

Goals and scope

- Goal: Reduce customer-visible latency regressions during demand spikes while maximizing GPU utilization and minimizing cold-start cost.
- Scope: Predictive horizontal scaling (pool-level & tenant-slice), priority-aware eviction, burst-credit accounting, and associated dashboards and alerts. Does not cover node lifecycle provisioning (see gpu-pool-live-shrink runbook).

Ownership

- Primary owner: eng-platform (platform-scheduling subteam)
- Secondary owners: eng-infra (gpu-fleet team), eng-serving-runtime (runtime team)
- On-call rotation: platform-scheduling primary pager; escalation to gpu-fleet after 30 minutes if capacity cannot be recovered.

Key concepts and terminology

- predictive scaler: Service that forecasts 10m/30m/2h demand and suggests scale actions (predictive-scaler).
- eviction policy: Priority and fairness rules applied when GPU memory or compute is constrained.
- burst credits: Short-term capacity allowance for latency-sensitive tenants.
- KV cache warmup: Mechanism to prepopulate model KV caches after scale-up to reduce first-token latency.

Metrics and SLOs (what we observe)

- Core SLOs (global):
  - 99th-percentile response latency <= configured target for latency-sensitive models (default 750ms)
  - Error rate (5xx) < 0.2% per minute
- Capacity/utilization targets (internal):
  - Average GPU memory utilization target: 65%
  - Average GPU compute utilization target: 55%
  - Spare headroom target for burst: 10% of pool capacity

Essential metrics to stream into Prometheus/metrics pipeline:

- predictive_scaler.forecast_rate_{10m,30m,2h}
- scheduler_api.pending_queue_length
- gpu_pool.available_gpus
- gpu_pool.memory_headroom_percentage
- tenant_priority_burst_credit_{available,consumed}
- runtime.kv_cache_hit_rate
- inference_latency_ms_p50_p95_p99 (per model)

Dashboards (recommended panels)

1) Predictive Scaling Overview (grafana)
- Forecast vs actual QPS (10m, 30m)
- Scale actions timeline (scale-ups/scale-downs triggered by predictive-scaler)
- Pending start time distribution after scale-up (bucketed in seconds)

2) Eviction & Priority View
- Eviction count by reason (memory_pressure, preemption, node_failure)
- Evicted-tenant list (last 24h)
- Burst-credit balance heatmap by tenant tier

3) Cold-start & KV Warmup
- First-token latency for sessions that start after scale-up
- KV cache warmup success rate (jobs vs target)

Alerting and thresholds (Prometheus-style examples)

- Alert: predictive_scaler.misforecast_ratio > 1.25 for 3m
  - Meaning: Forecast is underestimating actual QPS by 25% or more. Action: investigate recent traffic changes, consider increasing forecast sensitivity or enabling immediate scale-up.
- Alert: gpu_pool.memory_headroom_percentage < 8% for 5m
  - Meaning: Low memory headroom; risk of OOM/ejections. Action: prepare eviction runbook steps and notify SRE.
- Alert: scheduler_api.pending_queue_length > 200 for 2m
  - Meaning: Backlog indicates throttling or insufficient capacity.

Sample PromQL (for alert translation)

- gpu_pool.memory_headroom_percentage < 8
- (sum(rate(inference_requests[1m])) by (pool) / predictive_scaler.forecast_rate_10m) > 1.25

Eviction policy and priority rules

Eviction is last-resort. Use the following ordered rules when memory/compute scarcity requires reclaiming:
1. Preempt best-effort low-priority tenants (tier = dev/batch) with oldest idle timestamp > 5m.
2. Reclaim ephemeral worker slots with no in-flight requests (safe to terminate immediately).
3. If still constrained, preempt lowest-priority latency-sensitive sessions with active fallback model configured.
4. As a final fallback, trigger graceful throttle for top consumers and notify product SLO owners.

Priority attributes considered:
- tenant_tier: enterprise | production | dev | batch
- model_latency_sensitivity: high | medium | low
- burst_credit_balance: numeric (clients with no credit are lower priority)

Runbook: Incident — sudden spike causing memory headroom < 5%

1) Pager fires on gpu_pool.memory_headroom_percentage < 8% sustained 5m.
2) On-call acknowledges within 5m and posts to #platform-ops with summary and runbook link.
3) Investigate: check predictive_scaler.forecast_rate and recent traffic source (kafka/topic, api-gateway logs).
4) If forecast undershot, trigger immediate scale-up (CLI: rk scale pool --pool-id <id> --add-gpu 2).
5) If scale-up unavailable or slow, run eviction step 1 (preempt dev/batch tenants):
   - CLI: rk eviction run --pool <id> --policy preempt-dev-batch --dry-run=false
6) After evictions, monitor inference_latency_p99 and error_rate for 10m.
7) If errors persist, escalate to gpu-fleet on-call and consider rolling restart of scheduler-api (safe window: low traffic periods only).
8) Prepare post-incident notes with timeline and corrective actions. Add to retrospective board.

Operational runbook: graceful scale-up with KV warmup

1) predictive-scaler computes a recommended scale-up for pool-A of +3 GPUs.
2) scheduler-api reserves slots and instructs gpu-orchestrator to allocate instances (k8s/GKE workers or on-prem node allocator).
3) Once nodes are healthy, run KV warmup jobs (job template below) against warmup-queue to prepopulate KV cache for high-priority models.
4) Only publish new capacity to tenant routing (router-service) after kv_warmup.success_rate >= 95% or 60s elapsed.

KV warmup job sample (yaml snippet):

apiVersion: v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: kv-warmup-job-pool-A-{{timestamp}}
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: warmup
        image: internal/warmup:stable
        args: ["--pool=pool-A","--models=baseline-list","--concurrency=8"]
      restartPolicy: Never

Configuration table (recommended defaults)

| config_key | default | notes |
|------------|---------|-------|
| predictive_scaler.lookback_window | 2h | training window for forecast model |
| predictive_scaler.sensitivity | 0.2 | fraction of predicted change that triggers immediate action |
| eviction.idle_threshold_seconds | 300 | min idle time before preempting dev/batch sessions |
| kv_warmup.concurrent_jobs | 4 | number of parallel warmup jobs per pool |
| burst_credit.default | 300 | seconds of burst credit for prod tenants |

Rollout checklist for changes to predictive-scaler or eviction logic

1) Feature branch and unit tests (include synthetic traffic tests).
2) Canary deploy to staging pool; replay 72h of production metrics and validate forecast error < 15%.
3) Deploy canary to a single small production pool during off-peak. Monitor dashboards for 1h.
4) Gradual rollout to remaining pools at 15-minute intervals. Abort if eviction count increases by > 20% over baseline.

Retrospective and continuous improvement items

- After each incident, fill short-form retrospective in the platform-retros board with: what happened, timeline, root cause, mitigations, and follow-ups.
- Quarterly review: compare forecast error distributions and consider model upgrades (LSTM -> Transformer time-series) where significant bias is observed.
- KPI to track improvement: p99 latency violations caused by capacity constraints (target down 50% in 6 months).

Implementation notes and tooling

- predictive-scaler implementation recommendations: use a layered approach — short-term ETS/Prophet for 10m/30m, and a light Transformer for 2h+ forecasts when data is available. Keep model evaluation lightweight and explainable.
- Use a feature-flag (feature.predictive_scaling_v2) to gate changes and allow fast rollback.
- All scale actions and evictions must be audit-logged to kafka topic: ops.cluster.actions (schema: timestamp, actor, pool_id, action, reason, effected_tenants[]).

Related pages

- /confluence/eng-platform/dashboards-and-alerts/platform-alert-routing-and-escalation-playbook-2026

Appendix: Postmortem template (short)

1) Summary: 1–3 sentences
2) Timeline: precise timestamps of detection, mitigation actions, and recovery
3) Impact: tenants affected, estimated client impact, SLA breaches
4) Root cause and contributing factors
5) Actions taken and owner assignments
6) Preventative measures and schedule for implementation

Contact and escalation

- On-call: #platform-pager (PagerDuty: platform-scheduling)
- Secondary escalation: gpu-fleet on-call (PD: gpu-fleet)
- Architecture consult: Linh Nguyen (eng-serving-runtime)

End of playbook
